# 1.0	System Architecture and Technology Stack

## 1.1	System Architecture Diagram

![][image1]  
*Figure 1 \- Detailed Architecture Diagram of the Apiary Smart System*

As all smart IoT systems usually include, this 4-layer architecture is fundamental to integrate the hardware and software seamlessly in order to display continuously-fed data to its user. The essence of this architecture is surrounded by the field nodes that are present in each hive as a microcontroller that the sensors are connected to, making this system very much scalable. From these nodes, the data flows through the gateways and is selectively chosen to be fed either through cloud or local data, however all real-time actuation is fundamentally done locally without cloud dependency \[1\].  
Firstly, the perception layer consists of both the sensors and actuators, clearly separated and categorized in Figure 1\. The selected environmental sensors are conjoined with the field nodes in the network layer that captures the data from it using multi-task scheduling in a uniform interval, about every 30 seconds, through FreeRTOS. The localized actuators are used for regulating the beehive’s microclimate in accordance to what type of environmental data it has captured from the sensors, keeping the hive’s health in its optimal state.  
The network layer establishes the local and wide-area data pipelines through the field node microcontrollers individually placed in each hive. These are then broadcasted using the ESP low-power Bluetooth Mesh stack (ESP-BLE-MESH), transferring data across the apiary yard towards the central IoT Standard Gateway which also uses an ESP32 but as a bridge. It uses WAN protocols such as the Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) in order to communicate between the devices in the perception layer and the data processing/management layer.  
The data processing layer acts as the central hub of our smart apiary system, held together by a local gateway provided by a Raspberry Pi that hosts a split database system, namely, a relational database that keeps apiary configurations and user authentication profiles for security, and a time-series database which actively logs every sensor data passed through. The Node-RED as seen in Figure 1 is described as the local control logic; this basically means that all data-driven tasks are handled by it in order to calculate threshold conditions and execute automation loops locally without internet latency. It links towards the cloud architecture, serving as both the data filter and translation \- what this means is that it filters only critical data to be sent to the cloud for deeper research that a local database cannot handle while also ensuring that data is formatted accordingly so that it can be read by the cloud platform.  
Lastly, the application layer is what gives users an interface in order to monitor and control the apiary system to their needs which can be provided by Grafana that is already native to the local gateway’s Raspberry Pi which displays real-time sensor graphs over the local area network. As an off-site solution, a mobile app is presented which practically handles quick checks on the hive status and provides push-notification alerts.

## 

## 1.2	Hardware Components

### 1.2.1	Core Components

The field node we selected that will become the hive’s microcontroller will be the **Espressif ESP32-S3**, as this specific chip includes hardware acceleration for neural network interfaces and hence can run deep learning. Many different studies have also shown the reliability of using ESP32 in similar systems, mainly for reasons such as low cost and robust integration \[2\]\[3\], which as a result enables it to become cost-efficient across multi-hive scales. As previously mentioned, we will be using FreeRTOS multi-task scheduling and also configure it to enter a deep sleep state between its 30-second sampling cycle to increase battery longevity and drop lower consumption, making it ideal for a self-sustaining solar panel operation \[4\].  
As for our local gateway that acts as our central edge hub, the most applicable hardware is the **Raspberry Pi 4**. This was chosen due to its capability of running a full Linux OS with the core IoT tools that we will use known as the MING stack, which includes Mosquito MQTT, InfluxDB, Node-RED and Grafana synchronously \- a study have also discussed such use cases in a hydroponics-based system, utilizing the same core hardware selection of an ESP32 along with the Raspberry Pi that uses this stack \[5\] which we can more or less integrate the same way, but just for a different purpose and using different sensors. We will also be making use of the **Geekworm X735 UPS** in tandem as an uninterruptible power supply to prevent local data loss and corruption.

### 1.2.2	Bio-Environmental Sensors

All these sensors are essentially connected into the field node, each individual sensor all connected to one field node per hive, to their respective pins.  
As a basic foundation for environmental sensors, the use of a **DHT22** module which captures the hive’s temperature and humidity acting as a climate monitor is used in this smart system as it delivers near-perfect accuracy. In addition, the use of a CO2 sensor such as the **MH-Z19B NDIR** is crucial for internal carbon dioxide tracking as high threshold levels infers many issues such as poor ventilation or high colony density. These sensors keep track of the health status of the beehive, monitoring conditions under the *optimum threshold of 30-36 degrees Celsius, 50-70% humidity, and 2500-3500ppm for CO2* \[6\] and serve as an early warning for any potential stressors or disruptance to the apiary.  
To capture data regarding honey flow, we can measure how heavy the beehives are. Using the **HX711** module, which is an explicitly designed high precision scale, and **four 50kg Load Cells**, which is essentially a pressure/weight detector that turns into electrical signals for the module to understand. This ensures constant monitoring of critical events such as honey flow, colony expansion \[6\] or even a hive theft. The four cells are placed in the four corners of the hive’s platform, preferably in the stand legs it sits on, carefully wiring it into the HX711 module.  
The usage of a microphone is for the sole purpose of recording and capturing the bee’s acoustic activity, which can be useful for estimating the status of a bee’s colony and behaviour which is detrimental when keeping honey production optimal \[7\]. For this, we can use the **INMP441 Digital MEMS Microphone**, as it features omnidirectional sound capture and uses a native digital I2S bus interface, entering our implemented ESP32-S3 free of static noise and maximizing prediction accuracy. We can mount the microphone on the inner wall of the hive body and encase it in a protective mesh to prevent propolis from bees while allowing clear sound transmission.  
As a means of monitoring bee traffic exclusively, we can use reflective IR pairs which incorporate both an infrared emitter and a phototransistor pair such as the **TCRT5000** that can be placed at the hive’s entrance to detect the bees going in and out instantaneously. With this information, the system can predict its foraging activity and roughly infer its flight behaviour which can be cross-validated with data captured from previously mentioned sensors.

### 1.2.3	Actuators

As sensor data flows through the system towards the data management layer, it sends it back in the form of automated control commands for the actuators to *act* upon, aiding in the regulation of the bee colony’s environment. This is provided by adding a ventilation system; the installation of this component is structurally integrated with a cooling fan alongside a servo motor that is used to autonomously push or pull a sliding shutter panel, completing the microclimate control loop \[8\]. The fan used should be a 5V brushless fan for its energy-efficient and advanced features option; it is used when it meets a certain critical condition, mapping a pulse-width-modulation (PWM) signal to control fan power accordingly. For the servo, a heavy-duty **MG996R** would be viable to work in a beehive condition where propolis is present. These components are strategically placed on the upper roof of the hive box as it allows for the stagnant hot air and CO2 to be exhausted out easily.  
Other actuators that are optional but strongly a recommended implementation are the buzzers and LED strip. The role of the buzzer is an alarm to notify of any theft or suspicious activity read from the sensors \- this can be achieved by using a simple **5V Active Piezo-Type Buzzer**. The buzzer should be placed within a reinforced compartment that is barely visible to avoid external tampering in the hive’s vicinity. The LED strip is used for visual hive status indicators for on-site visits, preferably using the **WS2812B Addressable NeoPixel** which will enable colored indicator output displays. This component should be placed where it is easy for the eyes to see, ideally right on top of the beehive, with a proper seal over it for better viewing.

## 

## 1.3	Software Platform Selection

Our proposed apiary automation setup utilizes a hybrid between edge and cloud, forming an edge-cloud architecture where real time sensing, short-term buffering, event detection and actuation control occur at the edge, while the cloud is used for long term storage, dashboard synchronization, remote access and model updates \[1\],\[30\]. This architecture is more suitable than an entirely cloud-based design, because apiaries generally operate in outdoor, distant environments where network instability is increasingly probable \[1\],\[31\] However, cloud utilization is still chosen to some extent over an entirely local system because of the cost and difficulty that comes with implementing a system capable of long term storage, constant synchronization, server-like access control and model (re)training \[31\],\[19\]. 

Looking at the edge layer of our architecture, we have chosen to center each of the hive nodes on the ESP32 Microcontroller. This is because the ESP32 efficiently integrates Wi-Fi and Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) in a compact, low-power format that is also used in other real-world bee-colony monitoring implementations \[2\],\[3\]. As described in Section 1.2, the ESP32 is chosen because it has sufficient power to effectively complete local tasks (acoustic preprocessing, lightweight intelligence, threshold-based control, sensor reading) without cloud reliance, making a good platform for the software which will run at each node \[3\],\[8\]. 

The software itself that will be run on each edge node is responsible for several of the key features planned for the smart apiary system. FIrstly, it acquires the raw data read by the DHT22 temperature-humidity sensor, the HX711 load cell module and the acoustic sensing module, alongside any of the secondary/extra sensors such as CO2 sensing or hive activity counts \[32\],\[8\]. After sensor reading collection, the software will perform preprocessing steps on the ingested data (calibration, smoothing, noise reduction and basic feature extraction) to ensure that possibly noisy raw data is converted into reliable monitoring information before being used for the more complicated tasks down the line \[3\],\[33\]. Lastly, threshold-based decision logic will be applied for microclimate regulation, abnormality detection and alerting systems (acoustic stress/swarm alerts) \[30\]. Having these core features on local software effectively allows the hive and apiary system to respond correctly and immediately, even during periods of internet instability \[1\],\[30\].

Moving towards the gateway and application integration layer, the system must use an IoT backend with MQTT compatibility. For this, AWS IoT Core is a suitable option because it was designed with secure connectivity, scalable publish-subscribe messaging protocols, and full-stack integration capability in mind, allowing it to support analytics, mobile dashboards and cloud connectivity, which are features we are utilizing in this apiary smart system \[18\],\[19\],\[20\]. However, in the proposed design, AWS IoT Core is only used for secure telemetry exchange, long term historical integration and remote application services, as real-time control is handled by the system edge \[1\],\[18\].

On the user interaction layer, a Flutter-based mobile application acts as the primary monitoring interface \[9\]. The mobile interface will be used as a dashboard, displaying both real-time and historical hive metrics such as internal temperature, humidity, weight, acoustic stress levels and alert logs. To ensure synchronization and reliability between the application and the incoming stream of sensor data, the application will be built on a structured state management approach, where a central state container receives the live data, and forces an update to the relevant dashboard displays when itself receives new data \[10\]. It will also deliver notification alerts for critical conditions like overheating, swarming risk, or any other dangerous abnormalities through cloud messaging \[15\]. 

Overall, the selected software platforms are justified for the apiary use case as it balances responsiveness, reliability, scalability and real-world deployment cost by keeping time-critical operations at the edge system, and only assigning storage, mobile synchronization and remote visualization to the cloud, solving the possible network instability that could occur on a farm, while ensuring the platform is robust enough for the possible future of advanced analytics, model training and scalability. 

## 

## 1.4	Communication Protocols

To support the smart apiary system design, our communication stack must support low-power local interaction, scalable telemetry, intermittent-connectivity tolerance and secure remote monitoring. Ensuring that we meet these requirements, we have chosen to implement a layered protocol strategy with BLE for local provisioning and short range node interaction, and MQTT over Wi-Fi for gateway-to-cloud telemetry and application-level communication \[2\],\[11\]. Relying on this dual protocol stack allows for lightweight, low-cost local connectivity alongside internet-facing remote access without forcing every action to depend on a persistent cloud link \[1\],\[31\].

BLE is suitable for local connectivity because it is natively supported by the ESP32 that we are using for the system, and is optimized for short-range, low-power communication between devices \[2\],\[32\]. Additionally, BLE can be used during installation or maintenance to easily register hive node or device identifiers, tune parameters and diagnose sensor behaviour using another device without requiring a full internet implementation \[2\],\[23\]. Should the deployed system ever scale to a denser multi-hive configuration, the BLE connectivity can be added to a mesh (BLE Mesh), allowing the infrastructure to remain reliant on BLE and easily scale, as BLE Mesh natively supports coordination between nodes while still preserving the present gateway \[23\].

For our cloud-facing communication, MQTT over Wi-Fi has been selected as the main application layer protocol, because of it's wide adoption and light-weight public-subscribe architecture, which minimizes overhead and prioritizes effectiveness for constrained embedded devices (like sensors) that needed to send frequent but small telemetry updates \[11\]. For this project, each of the hive nodes will be allowed to publish their relevant data in structured topic format to the network, while dashboard or notification components only subscribe to the data which they are meant to display, optimizing the flow of data and reducing network load \[11\],\[14\].

This publish-subscribe model that our design utilizes is especially suitable for the smart apiary because it separates sensory devices from the user applications, reducing load and bi-directional data transfer to only what is needed across the network \[11\],\[14\]. It also enables message prioritization, where emergency events can be published almost instantly, with a high priority that makes the dashboard components subscribe to them before any other data in the stream \[1\],\[30\].

To complete the network stack, Wi-Fi is used as the up link transport because of the ESP32's native Wi-Fi support, and because the apiary design is positioned in at least a semi-urban setting where internet infrastructure is more readily available than in the countryside or rural areas \[1\],\[32\]. However, because possible instability is always a possibility, Wi-Fi is reserved only for gateway synchronization and cloud communication, as they are non time-critical tasks, ensuring that edge-based logic can continue operating even when Wi-Fi is unstable \[1\],\[31\]. In practice, this means that the edge nodes or gateways will temporarily cache data during outages, then upload the buffered data once connectivity is restored, improving resilience and preventing loss of monitoring data \[1\],\[30\]. 

Lastly, to address security concerns across the network, MQTT traffic will be protected using Transport Layer Security, X.509 device certificates and topic-level access control lists so that only authorized components of the system can subscribe or publish to the apiary's data stream \[18\],\[21\]. 

## 

## 1.5	Data Storage and Management

To efficiently store and manage the continuous flow of timestamped sensor readings, derived risk indicators, actuator states and logs from the apiary design, we've chosen to implement a time-series database rather than a conventional transactional database because the data to manage and store is sequential, multi-sensory and strongly time dependent \[12\],\[35\]. As time-series storage is specifically optimized for this kind of use case, we will be capable of frequent writes and chronological aggregation, which are both central features of the apiary system proposed \[12\], \[13\].

To accommodate this design, InfluxDB will be chosen as our platform, as it is suitable for long-term storage and purpose-built for time series workloads, so it supports efficient querying and storage of timestamped telemetry data \[12\],\[13\]. This is especially important for our smart apiary design, because useful insight is almost always derived from trends over time rather than single readings, so being able to store, query and extract data across long periods of time is paramount \[7\],\[33\].  

To additionally ease the data analysis later on, stored data will be organized into four main categories \[24\],\[32\]. First is raw, preprocessed telemetry data. Second is derived analytics, such as swarm-risk scores, threshold-based alerts and ventilator control states generated by the ESP32 edge microcontroller. Third is event and alert history, which records abnormal incidents and their associated timestamp. Lastly is metadata, which includes the data such as firmware version, hive identifier and synchronization timestamps, which can be used as a tool for device management and diagnosis.

Within the database itself, a structured schema with tags and fields will be implemented to improve maintainability and usefulness of the analytics captured. For example, tags such as hive\_id, datetime, and sensor\_type allow the system to compare multiple unique hive nodes, group/filter sensors and aggregate data across time periods easily, while the actual fields only store actual values \[12\]. This structure makes dashboard queries simpler and more efficient, while also allowing for easy ingestion into machine learning workflows and model tuning, as they usually require clean sequenced data (time-series data for forecasting) \[3\],\[7\].

To ensure consistency with the initial hybrid edge-cloud architecture and reduce initial deployment cost, data management is divided between local buffering and cloud persistence. The edge nodes keep storage of only recent measurements, while long-term, permanent data is stored only on the cloud for remote access, historical analysis and hive node comparisons, uploaded from the edge in batches rather than live, reducing unnecessary uplink traffic because non-critical telemetry can be uploaded in batches, though high-priority alerts will be transmitted immediately \[1\],\[31\]. In the case of network disruption, the data batch intended for upload to the cloud is instead used as an expanding buffer that uploads to the cloud when network stabilizes, preventing data loss \[11\]. 

Lastly, to address data protection concerns, stored telemetry data and event logs are protected, and can only be accessed through authenticated services, while transmissions remain encrypted, implementing role-based permissions that restrict who can view or manage the hive data \[13\],\[17\]. Authentication of verified users and technicians will be handled through an identity provider, while data stored in the cloud will rely on server-side encryption \[16\],\[26\]. This is the best choice for our proposed use case and design, as (semi) urban apiary data can carry operational, geographic and commercial value that could even possibly be abused by competing apiaries, especially if deployment is expanded into larger operations \[1\],\[30\].

Overall, the proposed data storage and management strategy described above ticks all the boxes required by the apiary system, allowing for continuous, timestamped, multi-modal data that can be easily queried, stored and analyzed within a time-series database built with a structured schema in mind, and secured using various suitable authentication strategies, ensuring that the overall apiary system becomes robust, secure and scalable \[1\],\[12\],\[30\].

# 

# 2.0	Algorithm Design and Implementation

## 2.1 Control Algorithms

The control algorithms translate sensor measurements into actions to help keep beehives healthy. Rather than just logging environmental information for later analysis, the system uses the information gathered to regulate cooling fans, servo controlled air vents, estimate honey production and trigger alarm messages. Some hive conditions call for immediate action so most decisions are made on the Raspberry Pi gateway before the data is sent to the cloud. This edge-cloud design enables the gateway to act in real-time for control purposes and enables the cloud to store historical data and provide long-term analysis \[1\].

### 2.1.1 Microclimate Regulation

One of the most critical functions of this system is to keep the hives as stable as possible. A dramatic shift in temperature, humidity or CO₂ levels can cause stress to the bee colony and affect the overall health of the colony. The system periodically gets data from DHT22, DS18B20 and CO₂ sensors to monitor these conditions. These environmental measures are most commonly used in the beehive monitoring process as they give a good indication of the state of the colony \[6\].  
The system then reads the values from the sensors and compares them with the different operating ranges. If the temperature begins to rise too much, the servo-controlled air vents open up and the cooling fans speed up to cool down. When it gets below the desired temperature the vents close and the fans stop, allowing heat to stay within the hive. Humidity is controlled in a similar manner. The vents open more with increased humidity and close to the lowest setting when humidity is lower, to minimize moisture loss. The levels of carbon dioxide are monitored separately. When it is over the safe limit, it starts to ventilate although it is not too hot. These fans and servo vents are thus responsible for maintaining the internal hive environment in concert \[8\].  
The system also prevents any unwarranted movement of the actuator. There are no immediate large-scale changes in response to small environmental changes. When the PID is operating normally the temperature is measured and compared to the target temperature, and the fans and air vents are slowly moved to reduce the temperature difference. Such a method offers a more gentle environmental control than an on-off control method and also helps to decrease mechanical abrasion \[8\].

### 2.1.2 Swarm & Theft Alert Algorithm

The system also tracks any potential swarming and theft of the hives to ensure the safety of the colony. The condition in the hive is constantly varying naturally during the day, so relying on one sensor would give unreliable results. Audio recordings are influenced by both the activity of bees and ambient noise; hive weight fluctuates when bees go out and come in. The algorithm therefore analyzes a number of indicators in combination, such as the weight of the hives, the sound of the colony, the activity of the bees entering the hives and the time of day. In the past, it has been demonstrated that such a combination of signals for swarm detection can be beneficial \[6\]\[7\].  
The information from each sensor will be different and will influence the decision. Load cells detect any abrupt drops in hive weight. Small weight losses result in a low level warning, and large and rapid losses could be the sign of hive theft or movement. At the same time, microphones constantly record the sounds from the colony. Event Score is incremented if the audio classification model detects PRE\_SWARM / STRESSED behaviour. Entrance sensors are also a source of information. Bees that are not active during the day may mean that the hive situation is abnormal. All evidence combined by the system in order to detect an event with more reliability than by using only one sensor \[6\]\[7\].  
Then an Event Score is calculated to decide on the appropriate response. If the weight loss is in addition to a high score, a theft alarm is sounded and the local buzzer operates. If the score is primarily due to abnormalities in the acoustic patterns, the system instead alerts with a pre-swarming warning. Lower scores are not necessarily an alert. It is only recorded, then the hive is checked again several minutes later. This approach helps minimize false alarms and improves user responsiveness to regular alarms \[6\]\[7\].

### 2.1.3 Honey Yield Estimation

The system can also estimate the production of honey based on hive weight measurements in addition to environmental monitoring. The weight of the hive does not measure the amount of nectar or honey stored in the hive, but it can be used as a practical estimate since the weight of the hive continually increases as the nectar or honey is stored. The algorithm does not take into account day-time weight measurements as the bees move around a lot in the day causing more noise in the measurement. Nighttime hive weight has also been used as a proxy for the honey flow and the state of the colony in previous IoT research \[6\].  
As part of the gateway's nightly routine, the average weight of the hives is computed over a period of several hours, and compared to the average weight from the previous night. If this steady increase occurs over several days then there is a honey flow, and the mobile app will inform the beekeeper. A continued decline in the average weight may indicate that the colony is drawing on its food reserves and supplemental feed should be offered. This will enable the beekeepers to observe the productivity of the colony without opening the hive frequently \[6\].

## 

## 2.2 Data Processing & Analysis

However, for sensor measurements to be useful to either help make a control decision, or to allow the user to monitor the measurements, they need to be processed to yield information that is reliable. Outdoor conditions have a number of factors that contribute to measurement error, such as rain, wind, high humidity, erratic power supplies and loose power connections. Therefore, the system validates, cleans and organizes the raw data before storing it and presenting it using the mobile application. These tasks can be performed locally as well, which speeds up the response time and decreases the unnecessary communication with the Cloud \[1\]\[6\].

### 2.2.1 Data Filtering & Cleaning

Any data analysis is preceded by checking the data quality. The system does not take all sensor readings as it comes but compares the new reading with the recent reading. Readings which are significantly different from the recent average will be flagged as outliers as these readings are more likely to be caused by sensor problems than environmental changes. The elimination of these abnormal values eliminates the chance of erroneous control actions due to incorrect measurements \[6\].  
The gateway is also responsible for monitoring the status of operation of each sensor node. The heartbeat message is sent periodically (every couple of minutes) by each node. The node is considered offline if no heartbeat is received for a long time and no more control commands are sent to this node. Windy weather causes extra filtering of audio recordings because wind noise can make analysis of the sounds less accurate \[6\]\[7\].

### 2.2.2 Data Aggregation

After data cleaning, the data is transformed to summaries for long-term monitoring. Sensors may report a reading every 30 seconds but keeping track of each individual reading would be problematic, both in terms of storage and application performance. This means that the recent raw data will be stored in the gateway for short-term view, and that the gateway will compile 5-minute, hourly and daily summaries for historical analysis. This processing technique is similar to many IoT monitoring systems which relies on MQTT, Node-RED, InfluxDB and Grafana to process continuous streams from sensors \[5\].  
The daily reports give an overall picture of the status of the hives. Each report contains a minimum, a maximum and an average of the temperature, the humidity, the CO₂ concentration, the weight of the hive, the weight change, the entrance bee activity and the results of the audio classification. The long-term trends are much easier to see than the vast number of raw sensor readings \[6\] using these summaries.

### 2.2.3 Data Visualization

The information is processed, and presented through the mobile application in an easy to understand format. Each hive will appear on its own Hive Card with temperature, humidity, CO₂ concentration, weight, audio status, actuator status and health score. This will enable users to identify which hives need to be tended to, instead of having to look at individual sensor readings \[6\].  
There are also various graphical views available for more detailed monitoring. Changes in the amount of honey flow are shown on weight trend charts, transitions between the colony status (NORMAL, STRESSED, PRE\_SWARM) are recorded on audio timelines, and heat maps indicate multiple occurrences of overheating or insufficient ventilation. Such visualizations are useful for the users to better understand the changes in the behaviour of the colonies over time \[6\]\[7\].

### 2.2.4 Machine Learning Analysis

Machine learning is mainly applied to hive audio analysis. The ESP32-S3 extracts features from the audio signal locally, without uploading the entire audio file to the cloud. The system processes sound frequencies, extracts Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) and classifies the sound recordings as NORMAL, STRESSED, PRE\_SWARM or QUEENLESS. These classifications offer some clues as to colony condition and potential swarming activity \[7\].  
The cloud enables the classification model to be continually improved. Beekeepers validate the accuracy of the alerts and as more data is available, the labelled data is used to retrain the model. The updated models are then sent back to the gateway and sensor nodes. This process enhances the accuracy of detection of the local apiary conditions while maintaining the rapid response provided by edge computing \[1\]\[3\].

## 

## 2.3	Mobile App Functionality

### 2.3.1 Real-Time Monitoring

The main screen of the mobile application displays all managed beehives in the network format dashboard. Each beehive represents its own card, so beekeepers can quickly check the current condition of the apiary without opening each beehive one by one to check \[9\], \[10\]. Each card will show the latest temperature, humidity, weight and sound-based beehive status labels, and then a score will be given with an overall health of 0 to 100 \[9\], \[10\]. This can make it more convenient and faster for beekeepers to grasp the status of the peak nest.  
When the user clicks on the beehive card he wants to observe, the application will open the detailed view of the selected beehive \[9\], \[10\]. This page contains real-time charts of all sensor readings, and each chart is updated every five seconds \[10\], \[11\]. Therefore, beekeepers can observe changes almost immediately without reading outdated readings.  
The details page also shows the current actuator status, including servo angle, fan PWM working cycle and buzzer status. This helps users understand how the automation system responds to the current sensor data. A small connection badge also shows whether the application is in "local" mode or "remote" mode \[9\], \[10\]. In local mode, the application and Raspberry Pi agent are connected using WebSocket-MQTT. In remote mode, when a user leaves the Apiary, the application will use REST to connect through AWS \[13\], \[14\]. These two modes are switched between local and remote mode automatically, so the user doesn't have to worry about the connection.  
If the beehive node stops sending heartbeat signals, the beehive card will turn gray and display the "offline" badge \[12\], \[14\]. It will also show the last time the data was received \[12\], \[14\]. This makes it easier for connection or device problems to be noticed, rather than relying on users to be aware of missing data.

### 2.3.2 Remote Control

Besides monitoring, the app also allows users to control the hive hardware remotely \[12\]. The actuator override panel includes a servo slider from 0° to 180°, a fan speed slider from 0% to 100%, and a buzzer test button. Each command is sent through MQTT to the selected hive’s command topic, which helps keep control commands separated between different hive devices \[12\].  
Each hive also has its own Auto/Manual toggle. In Auto mode, the control algorithm manages the actuators based on the sensor readings. In Manual mode, the actuator stays at the setting chosen by the user. This gives beekeepers more control when they need to make direct adjustments.  
To avoid unsafe situations, Manual mode has a 30-minute safety timeout. For example, if ventilation is left fully open by mistake, the system will automatically return to Auto mode after the timeout. Administrators also have an extra function through an OTA trigger button, which allows them to manually send firmware updates to selected hive nodes when needed \[27\], \[28\].

### 2.3.3 Scheduling

Although remote control action is very effective, scheduling can help beekeepers set rules for automatic operation. These rules are based on time or conditions, so the system does not need to be monitored all the time. For example, beekeepers can set a rule to turn on the ventilation every morning in every hot month. The schedule of these rules will be stored in InfluxDB, continuously observed by Node-RED, and run on the gateway \[11\], \[15\].  
The application also supports inspection reminders according to the weight threshold of the beehive \[11\]. For example, beekeepers set a weight threshold of 38 kilograms, and when the hive reaches that weight, the application will remind them to harvest honey as soon as possible before the frame is full \[11\].  
There is also a feeding reminder function. This works by checking the foraging conditions. If the system finds that the availability of nectar is low for more than three consecutive days, it will notify the user that additional feeding is . This helps to turn the sensor mode into a useful reminder instead of expecting beekeepers to interpret all the data manually.

### 2.3.4 Notifications and Alerts

Alerts will be sent through Firebase Cloud Messaging and are divided into different levels of severity \[15\]. This can ensure that users will not be reminded by unnecessary alerts many times, and will still receive reminders when something important happens.  
Key alerts include theft detection, thermal emergencies and dangerous high carbon dioxide levels. These alarms will trigger sound and vibration, so even if the mobile phone is not in your pocket or around, it will be difficult to miss the reminder. Warnings include swarm risk, offline nodes and cold stress conditions. These are displayed as silent badge notifications, which means that they are visible but will not cause too much interference. Information alerts, such as the beginning of honey flow activities, harvest readiness or nectar shortage period, appear in the form of banner notifications. These provide useful updates, but not important yet to take immediate actions.  
Each notification will contain hive ID, reading of sensor at the time of the alarm, and location of the beehive marked by GPS. This is effective for beekeepers that manage beehives in different places, because they can quickly know where the problem is happening. The application will also keep a local alert history in the log of the device, including whether each alert is turned off. The log can be exported as a CSV file, which can be useful when using for insurance claims, veterinary records, or future colonial health documents.

### 2.3.5 Personalisation

The design of the application is suitable for different beekeepers because of their different management methods. Therefore, instead of using the same fixed settings for everyone, they are able to adjust settings according to their own preferences.  
Users can customize their own alarm threshold. For example, when a beehive reaches a pre-defined weight, then honey is ready to harvest. These rules are stored in the user account in the AWS Cognito profile attributes, so even if the user changes the device, adds a device or logs in again \[16\], \[17\], the settings can still be used as long as the settings are in the same account.  
Users can also provide a custom name for the hive node, record the introduction date of the queen bee, and add beekeeper comments. This information is stored in the InfluxDB cloud metadata bucket together with the sensor data.  
The application also uses role-based access controls. Administrators have full access rights, including the ability to control the actuator, adjust the alarm threshold and trigger OTA firmware updates. Viewer-level users can only view the dashboard and cannot control the hardware. This access control is managed by AWS Cognito user pool membership \[16\], \[17\].  
In order to save records, users can generate monthly PDF colony health reports for a single beehive. If data is required for academic research, reports or regulatory purposes, they can also export the original data as XLSX files.

## 2.4	Security Considerations

### 2.4.1 Device Authentication

Each ESP32-S3 hive node will have its own unique X.509 client certificate. This certificate is issued by a private certificate authority registered in AWS IoT Core \[18\], \[19\]. Therefore, each device has its own identity, and not all devices share common credentials.  
When the device is connected to AWS IoT Core through MQTT, it uses mutual TLS\[19\]. This means that the device must use its certificate to prove its identity to AWS IoT Core. At the same time, the device also uses the embedded Amazon Root CA 1 certificate to check back the server certificate of AWS. This is helpful for both parties to start communicating after proper verification.  
For the local BLE Mesh network, new nodes can only be added through configuration applications with correct pre-shared AppKey. Without a network key, unconfigured devices are not able to join the grid \[20\]. This reduces the risk of fake or unauthorized devices being added to the system network.  
Human users will be authenticated separately through the AWS Cognito user pool. Mobile applications use OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE. This provides a short-lived JWT access token that expires after an hour, as well as a refresh token that is valid for 30 days. This shows that even if the access token is stolen, the usage time is only capped at one hour \[16\], \[17\].

### 2.4.2 Data Encryption

Encryption is applied across the whole system, both when data is moving between devices and when it is stored. This helps protect the data at every stage instead of only securing one part of the network.

*Table 1: communication channel and its encryption standard it uses*

| Communication Channel | Encryption Standard |
| ----- | ----- |
| BLE Mesh (hive node ↔ gateway ESP32) | AES-CCM 128-bit \[22\] |
| Local MQTT (bridge ESP32 → Mosquitto) | TLS 1.2 with username/password credentials \[21\] |
| Cloud MQTT (Pi → AWS IoT Core) | TLS 1.3 with X.509 mutual authentication and AES-256-GCM cipher suite \[18\] |
| Data at rest — local InfluxDB | LUKS AES-256 filesystem encryption on Raspberry Pi SSD \[14\] |
| Data at rest — cloud InfluxDB | AWS-managed AES-256 server-side encryption with KMS-managed keys \[26\] |
| ESP32 NVS (device configuration) | AES-XTS 256-bit NVS encryption |
| Mobile app ↔ AWS | HTTPS TLS 1.3 with AWS Cognito JWT bearer token |

Overall, this means the data is not sent or stored in plain text. From the moment a sensor reading leaves the hive node, passes through the gateway and cloud services, and finally appears on the mobile app, encryption is used to protect it.

### 2.4.3 Access Control

Access control is applied at several levels in the system. The system follows the principle of minimum privileges instead of relying on a security checkpoint. This means that each device, service or user can only get the access it needs. In order to prevent one hive node from damaging or affecting the data of other hive nodes, at the core level of the AWS IoT, each device certificate is associated with the minimum privilege IoT policy \[18\]. A hive node only allows data and status messages to be published to its own topics, and can only subscribe to its own commands and OTA topics. Subjects of other devices are not allowed.  
On the Raspberry Pi gateway, the Mosquitto ACL file provides its own special username for each BLE Mesh bridge ESP32 \[21\]. Each bridge is only allowed to publish and subscribe within its assigned topic hierarchy. Node-RED acts as the brain on this gateway. It is a process that uses a separate account with more permissions, because it needs to coordinate a wider range of gateway functions.  
In the Flutter application, role-based access control separates administrators from viewer-level users. Administrators can control the actuator, change the threshold and trigger OTA updates. The audience can only access the read-only dashboard. Importantly, this restriction is checked on the server side through the Cognito group membership of the API layer. This means that viewers cannot bypass restrictions just by trying to call the API directly \[16\]. Considering physical safety. The Raspberry Pi 4 gateway is placed in the IP65-grade outdoor shell and equipped with a physical lock. Its USB and HDMI ports are also disabled at the operating system level through /boot/config.txt and raspi-config. When someone actually accesses the device, it helps to reduce the risk of local tampering.

### 2.4.4 Firmware Updates

The OTA firmware update process is safe from beginning to end. This is very important because the hive node is a device with limited resources and can be operated on site without continuous supervision \[23\].  
This process begins from the construction stage. The new firmware is compiled through the GitHub Actions CI pipeline. After the firmware binary file is generated, the SHA-256 hash will be generated. Then use the Ed25519 private key securely stored in the hardware security module through AWS CloudHSM\[29\] to sign the binary file. This ensures that the signature key is not exposed to the secure environment. After signing, the firmware file and its separate Ed25519 signature are uploaded to the private and versionized AWS S3 bucket \[26\].  
To start updating, the gateway will send an MQTT OTA\_TRIGGER message to the OTA theme of the selected node. This message contains the new firmware version and the S3 pre-signed URL. The URL will expire in 15 minutes, which helps prevent the same download link from being reused in a replay attack.  
ESP32 uses the esp\_https\_ota library \[25\] to download the firmware through HTTPS. Its TLS certificate is fixed on Amazon Root CA 1\. Before receiving the update, the device uses the public key stored in its read-only flash memory to check the SHA-256 checksum and Ed25519 signature. If any verification fails, the update will be canceled, and the device continues to run the latest existing verified firmware.  
The system also uses A/B partition settings with factory partitions, OTA\_0 and OTA\_1. The newly installed firmware has 60 seconds to prove its functionality by calling esp\_ota\_mark\_app\_valid\_cancel\_rollback() after the first start, or else the boot loader will roll back to the last working partition \[24\]. This prevents failed updates for permanently damaging the device on site.  
In addition, the use of RSA-PSS 3072-bit signature enables secure boot V2 at the hardware level. This is the configuration recorded through eFuse during the initial configuration \[27\]. Because the ROM boot loader verifies the signature before running any code, the unsigned firmware cannot run even if the attacker physically removes the flash memory chip and tries to refresh it again.
